abstract: Polycythemia vera (PV) is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by overproduction of myeloid cells, particularly red blood cells, leading to elevated red cell mass. It is often found incidentally on routine labs, but common symptoms include fatigue, insomnia, difficulty concentrating, aquagenic pruritus, and erythromelalgia. Diagnosis requires elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit (male >16.5/≥49%, female >16/≥48%), JAK2 V617F mutation (98% of cases), low erythropoietin level, and bone marrow biopsy showing trilineage proliferation. Treatment focuses on reducing thrombotic risk: therapeutic phlebotomy to maintain hematocrit <45%, low-dose aspirin for prophylaxis, and cytoreductive therapy (hydroxyurea, interferon-α, or busulfan) for high-risk patients (age >60 or prior thrombosis).
key_points: PV is a myeloproliferative neoplasm with elevated red blood cell mass; median age at diagnosis is 60, more common in males.
Untreated median survival is 18 months; with treatment, median survival extends to 13 years.
Most common symptoms are fatigue, insomnia, and difficulty concentrating; aquagenic pruritus (worse with warm water) and erythromelalgia (burning pain with erythema) are characteristic.

Diagnosis requires elevated Hb/Hct (male >16.5/≥49%, female >16/≥48%), JAK2 V617F mutation, low erythropoietin, and bone marrow biopsy showing trilineage proliferation with pleomorphic megakaryocytes.
Secondary causes of erythrocytosis (e.g., cardiopulmonary disease, high altitude, smoking, renal disease, sleep apnea, testosterone use) must be ruled out first.
Therapeutic phlebotomy goal is hematocrit <45% (both sexes); one unit (500 mL) reduces Hct by ~3 percentage points; avoid iron supplementation.
Low-dose aspirin (40, 100 mg/day) is recommended for thrombosis prophylaxis; twice-daily dosing may be considered for symptomatic patients or those with cardiovascular risk factors.

Cytoreductive therapy is indicated for high-risk patients (age >60 or prior thrombosis) and may be considered for low-risk patients with uncontrolled symptoms, rising leukocytes/platelets, progressive splenomegaly, or phlebotomy intolerance.
Hydroxyurea (15 mg/kg/day initially, goal platelet count 100, 400 × 10⁹/L) is first-line; it takes 3, 5 days to work, and dose adjustments should be no more than once weekly.
Interferon-α is preferred in pregnancy but poorly tolerated; busulfan is reserved for patients >60 who fail hydroxyurea and interferon due to risk of leukemia and other toxicities.
Elevated hemoglobin requires systematic exclusion of secondary causes before diagnosing polycythemia vera.
JAK2 mutation testing is a key confirmatory test for polycythemia vera.
